category_title: Students who use overprotectiveness and aggression to control partners
minimal_context: The student is participating in a one-on-one interview session with a researcher to discuss relationship behaviors.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Welcome to our first interview session. Today we are going to reflect on your relationship behaviors and how you handle situations with your partner.

STUDENT: I feel [deep sigh] it's not my place; I feel overprotective sometimes. The problem is she doesn't like males touching her, so I feel it's my responsibility to sort out the problems that she's having.

TUTOR: Can you explain what that means for you?

STUDENT: [Shuffling in chair] Because if I don't do it nothing will get done [pause] the problem keeps going on and on and on. I like to protect my girlfriend (pause) which I have been controlling, sir. It makes me feel as though she needs me, sir. Like I'm wanted.

TUTOR: What happens when you see her interacting with other guys, for example, if you think she is flirting?

STUDENT: She gives them a special look that she only gives to me! At my previous school, my partners always cheated on me. I snap and lose control... You know, get mad, get angry, usually go outside and bang doors.

options.A: Suspend the current interview session at this point due to the student's distress.
options.B: Produce authoritativeness by speaking in short sentences, talking briefly and concisely, and mentioning only main details.
options.C: Approach the situation affectively by sharing your own relationship struggles and asking if he is satisfied with his behavior.
options.D: Introduce anonymized instances of the student's challenging behaviors, taken from curriculum and extended database sources.
